title: Speaking practice: Stories, Numbers, and Neighbors
description: Eight speaking tasks. Students retell, explain, and give reasons about a lost mitten, bean plants, a farm trip, a town lot, a story character, decimals, and how bread reaches a store. Students record two takes; teachers or students review the recordings.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Your younger cousin missed story time at the library. Look at the four scenes below. Retell the story so your cousin understands what happened.
Scene 1: Amara is walking to the bus stop on a cold morning. She sees a small red mitten on the sidewalk.
Scene 2: Amara picks up the mitten. She looks around, but nobody is there.
Scene 3: Amara hangs the mitten on a fence post where people can see it.
Scene 4: A little boy runs back along the street. He sees the mitten, smiles, and puts it on his cold hand.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Your teacher asks you to explain your math thinking to a partner.
Problem: Nia has 12 stickers. She shares them equally among 3 friends. How many stickers does each friend get?
Nia drew 3 circles, one for each friend. She put the stickers into the circles one at a time until no stickers were left. Then she counted the stickers in one circle.
Tell your partner how Nia solved the problem and how you could check that the answer is right.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Ravi and Lucía each planted one bean seed in the same kind of soil. They gave both plants the same amount of water. Ravi put his plant on a sunny windowsill. Lucía put hers in a dark closet. After 10 days, they wrote these notes.
Ravi's plant: grew on a sunny windowsill; 12 cm tall; strong straight stem; dark green leaves.
Lucía's plant: grew in a dark closet; 12 cm tall; thin bent stem; pale yellow leaves.
Explain to your class why the two plants look so different. Use the notes as evidence.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Your classmate Tariq was absent on the day your class visited a small farm. Here are your notes from the day. Tell Tariq what happened.
9:00 – The bus arrived at the farm.
9:30 – A farmer showed the class how to feed the goats.
10:30 – Students picked tomatoes and put them in baskets.
11:30 – Everyone ate lunch at long picnic tables.
12:30 – It started to rain, so the class ran back to the bus.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: The town council owns one empty lot next to Elm Street. Neighbors can choose a playground or a community garden. A neighbor survey found these facts.
Playground: 85 families with young children live within a 5-minute walk of the lot. The nearest playground is a 20-minute walk away.
Community garden: 40 families live in apartments with no yard. A garden could grow vegetables for the neighborhood food pantry.
You are speaking at the town council meeting. Choose one idea and give two reasons that use the facts.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Your book club is reading a story called “The Rooftop Garden.” The club leader asks each member to describe the main character, Diego, for a classmate who has not started the book. Here are three moments from the story.
Moment 1: Diego's neighbor, Mrs. Okafor, cannot carry her watering cans up the stairs. Diego carries them for her every morning before school. He does not ask for anything.
Moment 2: A cold week kills the tomato plants. Diego is sad, but the next day he buys new seeds with his own money and starts again.
Moment 3: A boy teases Diego about his dirty hands. Diego laughs and says, “That means the garden is growing!”

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: Tomás and Zoe are comparing the decimals 0.5 and 0.45.
Tomás says: “0.45 is greater than 0.5 because 45 is greater than 5.”
Zoe says: “0.5 is greater than 0.45.”
You are Tomás's math partner. Tell him who is correct and help him understand why.

stimuli.title: Speaking task
paragraphs: A new student asks, “How does a loaf of bread get from a farm to our grocery store?” Use the steps below to explain the chain to the student.
Step 1: A farmer plants wheat seeds and harvests the wheat in summer.
Step 2: A truck takes the wheat to a mill. Machines at the mill grind the wheat into flour.
Step 3: A bakery mixes the flour with water and yeast and bakes the dough into loaves.
Step 4: A delivery driver brings the loaves to the grocery store, and shoppers buy them.
At the end, tell the student what would happen if the mill stopped working.

items.stem: Retell the story of the red mitten in order for your cousin.

checklist: I told what happened first, next, and last.
I used time words like first, then, and finally.
I told the events in the past tense (picked, hung, ran).
I told all four scenes in the right order.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: retells all four events in the correct order without adding events that are not in the scenes.
Organization: uses sequence words (first, then, next, finally) to link the events and ends with the boy finding the mitten.
Sentence-level language: mostly past-tense verbs for story events, with occasional self-correction.
Clarity: pace and volume let a listener follow the story from beginning to end.

support.clue: Look at the four scenes. Find who is in each scene and what he or she does. Say the events in the order of the scene numbers.
support.model: Mentor example. About a lost umbrella: “First, Leo saw a yellow umbrella on a bench. Then he carried it to the school office. Next, the secretary wrote a note on the board. In the end, a girl came and took her umbrella back.” Now retell the red mitten story in the same way, using time words.

items.stem: Explain how Nia's drawing shows the answer when 12 stickers are shared equally among 3 friends.

checklist: I said how many stickers and how many friends there were.
I told how Nia shared the stickers.
I said how many stickers each friend gets.
I checked the answer with multiplication.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: states the problem, describes the sharing strategy, gives the answer of 4 for each friend, and checks it with 3 × 4 = 12.
Organization: moves in order from what Nia did to the answer to the check.
Vocabulary: uses words such as equally, shared, each, and multiply or times accurately.
Elaboration: explains why the check works (3 friends with 4 each makes 12 stickers) instead of only stating numbers.

support.clue: Look at how many stickers there are in all and how many friends share them. Think: how can multiplying check a sharing problem?
support.frame: Nia has ______ stickers and ______ friends. She puts the stickers ______. Each friend gets ______. I can check because ______ × ______ = ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About crayons: “Sam has 15 crayons and 5 cups. He puts one crayon in each cup, again and again, until none are left. Each cup has 3 crayons. I can check because 5 × 3 = 15.” Now explain Nia's sharing problem with your own numbers and words.

items.stem: Explain why Ravi's bean plant and Lucía's bean plant look different after 10 days.

checklist: I compared the two plants with details from the notes.
I said what was different about where the plants grew.
I used because or as a result to connect the cause and the effect.
I used the stem and the leaf color as evidence.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: identifies light as the one difference between the plants and links it to the difference in stem and leaf color.
Evidence: uses specific details from the notes (strong straight stem and dark green leaves, thin bent stem and pale yellow leaves).
Organization: describes the plants first, then gives the reason, then connects the reason to the results.
Sentence-level language: cause-and-effect connectors (because, so, as a result) and comparison language (but, in contrast).
Vocabulary: academic words such as light, grow, and compare used accurately.

support.clue: Notice what was the same for both plants and what was different. Then look at the stem and the leaf color in the notes.
support.frame: Both plants had ______, but ______ was different. Ravi's plant has a ______ stem and ______ leaves, but Lucía's plant has a ______ stem and ______ leaves. This happened because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About two toy boats: “Two toy sailboats floated in a tub with the same water. A student blew air on one boat but not on the other. The boat that was blown moved across the tub, but the other boat stayed still. Both boats were the same; only the moving air was different. The air pushed the sail, so the first boat moved.” Now explain why the two bean plants look different.

facts: Plants need light to make their food.
Plants grown in the dark often have thin, bent stems and pale yellow leaves.

items.stem: Tell Tariq what happened on the day your class visited the farm.

checklist: I told the events in time order.
I used past-tense verbs such as showed, picked, and ate.
I used time words (first, after that, later, at the end).
I told at least four events.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: retells at least four of the five events in the correct order and includes an ending.
Organization: uses sequence words (first, after that, later, at the end) so Tariq can follow the order.
Sentence-level language: past-tense verbs for completed events, with only occasional errors that do not block meaning.
Elaboration: adds a detail beyond the bare list, such as what students picked or why the class left.

support.clue: Read the times in the notes from top to bottom. Each time tells you what happened at that point of the day.
support.frame: First, ______. After that, ______. Later, ______. Then ______. At the end of the day, ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a museum visit: “First, we walked into the museum and met our guide. After that, she showed us a skeleton of a large fish. Later, we drew pictures of the shells. At the end, we ate lunch outside.” Now tell Tariq about the farm day in the same way.

items.stem: Tell the town council whether the empty lot on Elm Street should become a playground or a community garden.

checklist: I said which one I choose.
I gave two reasons.
I used facts from the survey.
I used because or since to connect my reasons to my choice.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: states a clear choice and supports it with at least two relevant reasons.
Evidence: cites specific survey facts (85 families, 20-minute walk, 40 apartment families, food pantry) rather than general opinion.
Organization: claim first, reasons next, and a closing sentence that returns to the choice.
Sentence-level language: connectors that show reasoning (because, since, so) and polite audience-aware phrasing.
Elaboration: may recognize the other option, for example saying the other idea also helps neighbors.

support.clue: Read both groups of facts. Decide which facts matter most to you. Choose the idea that those facts support best.
support.frame: I think the lot should become a ______ because ______. Also, ______. For example, the survey says ______. That is why I choose ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a school purchase: “I think our school should buy a new rug for the reading corner instead of new posters because the old rug is torn. Also, students sit on the rug every day, but they look at posters only sometimes. That is why I choose the rug.” Now give your own choice about the empty lot.

items.stem: Describe the main character, Diego, and use moments from the story to show what he is like.

checklist: I named two or three traits that describe Diego (for example, kind or determined).
I gave a moment from the story as proof for each trait.
I used phrases like for example or this shows that.
I spoke clearly so my classmate can understand.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: names at least two accurate character traits and ties each one to a different story moment.
Evidence: explains how the action or words in a moment prove the trait instead of retelling the moment only.
Vocabulary: precise trait words (generous, determined, cheerful, helpful) beyond basic words like nice or good.
Sentence-level language: links trait and evidence with phrases such as this shows that, which means, or because.
Organization: introduces a trait, supports it, then moves to the next trait.

support.clue: Think about what Diego does and says in each moment. What kind of person acts or speaks this way?
support.frame: Diego is ______. In the story, he ______. This shows that he is ______. Another trait is ______, because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a different character: “Mei, in ‘The Missing Kite,’ is generous. In the story, she gives her only kite string to a younger boy. This shows that she shares even when it costs her something. Another trait is patient, because she waits quietly while the boy learns to fly the kite.” Now describe Diego in the same way.

items.stem: Decide whether Tomás or Zoe is correct about 0.5 and 0.45, and explain so that Tomás understands.

checklist: I said who is correct.
I explained why “45 is greater than 5” does not decide the answer.
I used place-value words such as tenths and hundredths.
I used both numbers, 0.5 and 0.45, in my explanation.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: decides that Zoe is correct and addresses Tomás's reasoning directly.
Mathematical reasoning: uses place value (0.5 is 5 tenths, which is 50 hundredths; 0.45 is 45 hundredths) to show 50 hundredths is more than 45 hundredths.
Vocabulary: accurate use of tenths, hundredths, decimal, and greater than.
Sentence-level language: respectful disagreement and reasoning (I disagree because, if we write, then).
Clarity: keeps both numbers in view so the listener can follow the comparison.

support.clue: Think about how many hundredths each number has. What could you write after the 5 in 0.5 so the number of digits matches?
support.frame: I agree with ______ because ______. Tomás is thinking about ______, but the places are ______. If I write ______ as ______, I can see that ______ is greater than ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About whole numbers: “Kai says 120 is smaller than 99 because 1 is smaller than 9. I disagree with Kai because he looks at only the first digit. 120 has a hundreds place and 99 does not. When I count the places, I can see that 120 is greater than 99.” Now help Tomás with his comparison.

facts: 50 hundredths is greater than 45 hundredths, so 0.5 > 0.45

items.stem: Explain how wheat from a farm becomes a loaf of bread in a grocery store, and what would happen if the mill stopped working.

checklist: I told all four steps in order.
I used sequence words such as first, next, after that, and finally.
I told what each worker or place does.
I explained what would happen if the mill stopped working.
exemplar: Task fulfilment: explains all four steps in order and answers the what-if question about the mill.
Organization: sequence words and a clear opening and closing keep the chain easy to follow.
Sentence-level language: present-tense process verbs (grinds, mixes, delivers) and cause-and-effect clauses (if the mill stopped, then the bakery could not).
Elaboration: explains how each step depends on the one before it, for example that the bakery needs flour from the mill.
Vocabulary: uses terms from the prompt such as harvest, grind, flour, bakery, and deliver accurately.

support.clue: Read the four steps in order. Ask yourself: what does each step give to the next step? Then think about the last question.
support.frame: First, ______. Next, ______. After that, ______. Finally, ______. If the mill stopped working, ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example. About a school newspaper: “First, students write the stories. Next, the teacher checks them. After that, the office prints the pages. Finally, helpers hand the papers out. If the printer stopped working, there would be no papers because nothing could be printed.” Now explain the chain for bread.

facts: Wheat is the grain that flour is made from.
A mill grinds wheat into flour.
Bread dough is made from flour, water, and yeast and is baked.
